content: The availability of appropriate infection prevention and control (IPC) materials and equipment is critical for effective IPC programs in healthcare facilities. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized the importance of ensuring access to adequate water and sanitation services, a hygienic environment, and necessary materials and equipment as core components of IPC. These elements are essential for maintaining safe and effective healthcare delivery. Senior facility managers and local authorities are primarily responsible for maintaining a hygienic environment, but central governments and national IPC and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programs also play a significant role. They are tasked with developing standards and recommending the implementation of adequate WASH services, hygienic environments, and IPC materials at the point of care. In some cases, centralized production and distribution of supplies, such as alcohol-based hand rubs and soap by a national pharmacy, can be an effective approach. All healthcare facilities should provide the following: 1. Water and Sanitation: Access to water from an improved source located on the premises. Sufficient water available at all times for drinking, handwashing, food preparation, personal hygiene, medical activities, cleaning, and laundry. Hand hygiene facilities equipped with alcohol-based hand rubs and, where appropriate, water, soap, and disposable or clean towels at the point of care and within 5 meters of sanitation facilities. Functional sanitation facilities on the premises, including at least one toilet designated for women/girls to manage menstrual hygiene, one for staff, and one accessible to individuals with physical disabilities. 2. Hygiene and Waste Management: Adequate personal protective equipment (PPE) and puncture-resistant sharps containers, as well as containers for separating healthcare waste and cleaning supplies. Clean and hygienic conditions, including regular cleaning of examination rooms, waiting areas, surfaces, and toilets. Safe segregation, treatment, and disposal of healthcare waste, including autoclaving, incineration, or off-site treatment. Proper ventilation to reduce the risk of airborne pathogen transmission. Adequate drainage of storm and wash water to prevent vector breeding. Safe management of sewage and fecal waste through well-maintained septic tanks, leach fields, functioning sewers, or off-site removal. 3. Infrastructure and Energy: Adequate power for sterilization, incineration, and medical devices. Well-lit areas for healthcare procedures and toilet facilities, including at night. Sufficient energy for pumping water, sterilization, and operating healthcare waste equipment. Healthcare facilities must also address environmental factors associated with infection risks, particularly in acute care settings. The GDG highlighted the importance of involving IPC teams in the design, construction, and commissioning of new or upgraded healthcare buildings. This involvement is crucial during major renovations or demolitions to mitigate risks such as the release of airborne fungi, which can endanger patient safety. Key requirements for water supply and sanitation in healthcare facilities include: A continuous supply of safe water (5–400 liters per person per day, depending on the facility's needs). Safe water availability in treatment wards, waiting areas, and for drinking, handwashing, food preparation, personal hygiene, medical activities, cleaning, and laundry. Personal protective equipment (PPE), such as gloves, masks, goggles, face shields, and gowns, must be available in adequate quantities and stored in clean, dry areas to prevent contamination. Reusable items must have clear policies and procedures for decontamination. Decontamination of reusable items and medical devices is a complex process requiring dedicated areas and trained staff. Facilities must provide high-quality sterilization of critical clinical materials, supported by reliable energy sources. Isolation capacity is also vital, with single rooms or cohorting areas for patients with infectious diseases to prevent transmission. Effective waste management is essential to prevent the spread of infection. This includes proper segregation, collection, transportation, treatment, and disposal of healthcare waste. Adherence to environmental standards and compliance with national and international policies are necessary to maintain a clean and safe environment. Hand hygiene is a cornerstone of IPC and is critical for preventing healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Materials and equipment for hand hygiene, such as alcohol-based hand rubs and handwashing stations, should be readily available at the point of care. The WHO recommends a minimum of one handwashing basin per 10 beds and alcohol-based hand rubs at each point of care. The GDG strongly recommends ensuring the availability of IPC materials and equipment at the point of care, as evidence shows this increases compliance with good practices and reduces HAIs. Although the quality of evidence is low, the recommendation aligns with existing WHO guidelines on hand hygiene, which are widely implemented globally.
